Ovarian follicle maturation

Rodent studies report changes in follicle development and ovarian hormones, including more follicles and fewer cysts in a PCOS model. A small uncontrolled human pilot found a higher antral follicle count, but no significant increase in retrieved oocytes. No controlled clinical study has established improved human oocyte maturation or fertility (Naseri et al. 2017; Alves et al. 2019; Su et al. 2026).

PBM Database summary

What the records report

Rodent studies report changes in follicle development and ovarian hormones, including more follicles and fewer cysts in a PCOS model. A small uncontrolled human pilot found a higher antral follicle count, but no significant increase in retrieved oocytes. No controlled clinical study has established improved human oocyte maturation or fertility (Naseri et al. 2017; Alves et al. 2019; Su et al. 2026).

Summary of the Evidence

Four publications are relevant: one direct rat folliculogenesis experiment and three narrowly mapped ovarian studies in mature mice, PCOS rats, and aged mice. One mapped paper also included a 10-woman diminished-ovarian-reserve pilot, which is discussed under ovarian aging and is not an independent human replication. Follicle counts, oocyte competence, and completed maturation are related but distinct outcomes (Naseri et al. 2017; Oubiña et al. 2019; Alves et al. 2019; Su et al. 2026).

Human and clinical evidence

The 10-woman single-arm pilot reported a rise in median antral follicle count, but the number of retrieved oocytes increased only nonsignificantly. It did not establish that PBM caused more mature oocytes, successful fertilization, or pregnancy. No controlled human trial directly measuring follicle maturation was identified (Su et al. 2026).

Animal evidence

In a 28-rat comparison, ovarian irradiation with 810-nm near-infrared light produced greater follicular activity than 630-nm red light or clomiphene on several measured outcomes, including the number of oocytes. The authors presented the findings as a basis for further work, not as treatment evidence for human ovulatory disorders (Naseri et al. 2017).

A mature-mouse study found a higher percentage of primary and preantral follicles and AMH-positive early-stage follicles after treatment. It also reported lower progesterone, less apoptosis in early antral follicles, changes in ovarian vascular structure, and improved oocyte quality. A separate PCOS-rat study reported more follicles and corpora lutea, fewer ovarian cysts, and changes in reproductive hormones. The aged-mouse study found ovarian and pregnancy-related improvements with 630-nm red light, while its 850-nm arm did not show the same gains. The studies use different ages, disease models, wavelengths, and outcomes, so they should not be pooled as if they tested one protocol (Oubiña et al. 2019; Alves et al. 2019; Su et al. 2026).

Treatment Parameters and Generalizability

The direct rat study compared 630-nm red light with 810-nm near-infrared light at 5 J/cm² (Naseri et al. 2017). A mature-mouse study reported a fluence of 200 J/cm² (Oubiña et al. 2019). The aged-mouse study compared 630-nm with 850-nm LED exposure for 5 minutes daily over 15 days. Its small human pilot used an externally applied 630-nm LED before egg retrieval (Su et al. 2026). These protocols differ in species, dose, delivery, and model. No consistent optimum has been established, and a wavelength or dose that changes rodent follicle outcomes cannot be assumed to improve human oocyte maturation.

Interpretation

The animal literature shows changes in follicle development and related ovarian measures, with some outcomes moving in the direction of greater follicular activity. The human evidence remains limited to a small, uncontrolled follicle-count observation without a significant oocyte-yield improvement. A stronger conclusion requires controlled human studies that follow follicles through mature oocyte retrieval, fertilization, embryo development, pregnancy, and live birth.

Certainty of evidence (estimate)

Low certainty for follicular and hormonal changes in rodent models (Naseri et al. 2017; Oubiña et al. 2019; Alves et al. 2019; Su et al. 2026)

Very low certainty for human oocyte maturation and fertility outcomes (Su et al. 2026)

Rationale for the certainty assessment

The direct rat study and mapped rodent experiments report changes in follicle development, hormones, or oocyte quality, but they use different healthy, PCOS, and aging models. The only human report is a small uncontrolled pilot that measured follicle count and oocyte retrieval, not proven mature-oocyte or live-birth benefit. The evidence supports experimental ovarian changes, while the clinical effect remains uncertain (Naseri et al. 2017; Oubiña et al. 2019; Alves et al. 2019; Su et al. 2026).
